items.en: To pat, stroke, or pet gently.
items.note: 摸 mō (“to touch”) said twice. Doubling a verb like this makes it softer and more casual, so it comes across as “a little pat” or “give it a pet.” The second 摸 usually goes light and toneless, so it sounds like MŌ-mo. Common when petting an animal, or as a comforting pat on the head.
A common, cute use of 摸摸: a comforting pat on the head.

Slang from Cantonese (leng3 zai2), something like “good-looking dude” or “pretty boy.” Very common in Hong Kong and Guangdong; mainland internet slang picked it up too. People often use it playfully, even with strangers, the way you’d say “hey, handsome” or “hey bro.”
The female counterpart of 靓仔.
More common in Taiwan than 靓仔.
In messages, 你那边 often means “where you are” or “on your side.”
Use 还是 for “or” in questions. These questions already have 还是, so you don’t add 吗 at the end.

items.en: It's morning where you are. Are you tired?
items.py: Nǐ nà biān shì zǎo shang nǐ lèi ma
items.note: A more casual way to say it is 你那边是早上吧？累不累？ Here 吧 softens the guess, and 累不累 means “tired or not tired.”

items.py: Nǐ nà biān shì zǎo shang ba lèi bu lèi
items.note: A more casual version of 你那边是早上。你累吗？ 吧 softens the guess, and 累不累 means “tired or not tired.” 不 is often said lightly here: lèi bu lèi.

items.en: It's morning in Taiwan right now. Are you tired?
items.py: Tái wān xiàn zài shì zǎo shang nǐ lèi ma
items.note: If you're texting someone in Taiwan, they'll usually write it in traditional characters: 台灣現在是早上。你累嗎？

items.en: Are you drinking coffee or tea (right now)?
items.py: Nǐ zài hē kā fēi hái shì chá
items.note: 还是 already makes this a question, so you don't add 吗 at the end. In Taiwan's traditional characters: 你在喝咖啡還是茶？

items.en: Do you like coffee or tea?
items.py: Nǐ xǐ huan kā fēi hái shì chá
items.note: 还是 already makes this a question, so you don't add 吗 at the end. In Taiwan's traditional characters: 你喜歡咖啡還是茶？
